content.text: Read the following passage from Esperanza Rising. In this excerpt, Esperanza's grandmother, Abuelita, is teaching Esperanza how to crochet a blanket.

textContent.text: Esperanza's grandmother, whom everyone called Abuelita, lived with them and was a smaller, older, more wrinkled version of Mama. She looked very distinguished, wearing a respectable black dress, the same gold loops she wore in her ears every day, and her white hair pulled back into a bun at the nape of her neck. But Esperanza loved her more for her capricious ways than for her propriety. Abuelita might host a group of ladies for a formal tea in the afternoon, then after they had gone, be found wandering barefoot in the grapes, with a book in her hand, quoting poetry to the birds. Although some things were always the same with Abuelita—a lace-edged handkerchief peeking out from beneath the sleeve of her dress—others were surprising: a flower in her hair, a beautiful stone in her pocket, or a philosophical saying salted into her conversation. When Abuelita walked into a room, everyone scrambled to make her comfortable. Even Papa would give up his chair for her.
Esperanza complained, "Must we always crochet to take our minds off worry?" She sat next to her grandmother anyway, smelling her ever-present aroma of garlic, face powder, and peppermint.
"What happened to your finger?" asked Abuelita.
"A big thorn," said Esperanza.

pieces.text: Abuelita nodded and said thoughtfully, "
There is no rose without thorns."

textContent.text: Esperanza smiled, knowing that Abuelita wasn't talking about flowers at all but that there was no life without difficulties. She watched the silver crochet needle dance back and forth in her grandmother's hand. When a strand of hair fell into her lap, Abuelita picked it up and held it against the yarn and stitched it into the blanket.

"Esperanza, in this way my love and good wishes will be in the blanket forever. Now watch. Ten stitches up to the top of the mountain. Add one stitch. Nine stitches down to the bottom of the valley. Skip one."

Esperanza picked up her own crochet needle and copied Abuelita's movements and then looked at her own crocheting. The tops of her mountains were lopsided and the bottoms of her valleys were all bunched up. Abuelita smiled, reached over, and pulled the yarn, unraveling all of Esperanza's rows. "Do not be afraid to start over," she said.
Esperanza sighed and began again with ten stitches.
<citation>From Pam Muñoz Ryan, Esperanza Rising. Copyright 2000 by Pam Muñoz Ryan</citation>

pieces.text: Author Pam Muñoz Ryan had a grandmother who lived in Aguascalientes, Mexico and was named Esperanza Ortega.

content.text: In the novel, the characters of Abuelita and Esperanza possess traits similar to those of Muñoz Ryan's grandmother.

pieces.text: Some of the events are also drawn from real-life experiences Muñoz Ryan had with her grandmother.

content.text: For instance, Muñoz Ryan's grandmother taught her how to crochet using the same mountain and valley technique featured in the novel.

pieces.text: When Muñoz Ryan became an adult, she learned more about her grandmother's life. Muñoz Ryan recalls being surprised to know that her grandmother had been living like a princess in Mexico.

content.text: Her grandmother had been born into a wealthy family, but just like the fictional Esperanza, had to give it all up when she moved to work on the farm labor camps in California.

content.text: Read the following passage from Esperanza Rising. In this excerpt, Esperanza and her father walk through the family vineyard near their home in Aguascalientes, Mexico.

textContent.text: "Our land is alive, Esperanza," said Papa, taking her small hand as they walked through the gentle slopes of the vineyard. Leafy green vines draped the arbors and the grapes were ready to drop. Esperanza was six years old and loved to walk with her papa through the winding rows, gazing up at him and watching his eyes dance with love for the land.

"This whole valley breathes and lives," he said, sweeping his arm toward the distant mountains that guarded them. "It gives us the grapes and then they welcome us." He gently touched a wild tendril that reached into the row, as if it had been waiting to shake his hand. He picked up a handful of earth and studied it. "Did you know that when you lie down on the land, you can feel it breathe? That you can feel its heart beating?"
"Papi, I want to feel it," she said.
"Come." They walked to the end of the row, where the incline of the land formed a grassy swell.
Papa lay down on his stomach and looked up at her, patting the ground next to him.

Esperanza smoothed her dress and knelt down. Then, like a caterpillar, she slowly inched flat next to him, their faces looking at each other. The warm sun pressed on one of Esperanza's cheeks and the warm earth on the other.
She giggled.
"Shhh," he said. "You can only feel the earth's heartbeat when you are still and quiet."
She swallowed her laughter and after a moment said, "I can't hear it, Papi."

content.text: "Aguantate tantito y la fruta caerá en tu mano,"

pieces.text: he said. "Wait a little while and the fruit will fall into your hand. You must be patient, Esperanza."

textContent.text: She waited and lay silent, watching Papa's eyes. And then she felt it. Softly at first. A gentle thumping. Then stronger. A resounding thud, thud, thud against her body.

pieces.text: She could hear it, too. The beat rushing in her ears.

textContent.text: She stared at Papa, not wanting to say a word. Not wanting to lose the sound. Not wanting to forget the feel of the heart of the valley.
She pressed closer to the ground, until her body was breathing with the earth's. And with Papa's.

text.text: <atomic>"Our land is alive, Esperanza," said Papa, taking her small hand as they walked through the gentle slopes of the vineyard. Leafy green vines draped the arbors and the grapes were ready to drop.</atomic>
<atomic>Esperanza was six years old and loved to walk with her papa through the winding rows, gazing up at him and watching his eyes dance with love for the land.</atomic>
<atomic>"This whole valley breathes and lives," he said, sweeping his arm toward the distant mountains that guarded them. "It gives us the grapes and then they welcome us."</atomic>

<atomic>He gently touched a wild tendril that reached into the row, as if it had been waiting to shake his hand. He picked up a handful of earth and studied it. "Did you know that when you lie down on the land, you can feel it breathe? That you can feel its heart beating?"</atomic>
<atomic>"Papi, I want to feel it," she said.</atomic>
<atomic>"Come." They walked to the end of the row, where the incline of the land formed a grassy swell.</atomic>
<atomic>Papa lay down on his stomach and looked up at her, patting the ground next to him.</atomic>
<atomic>Esperanza smoothed her dress and knelt down.</atomic>
<atomic>Then, like a caterpillar, she slowly inched flat next to him, their faces looking at each other. The warm sun pressed on one of Esperanza's cheeks and the warm earth on the other.</atomic>
<atomic>She giggled.</atomic>
<atomic>"Shhh," he said. "You can only feel the earth's heartbeat when you are still and quiet."</atomic>
<atomic>She swallowed her laughter and after a moment said, "I can't hear it, Papi."</atomic>
"Aguantate tantito y la fruta caerá en tu mano," he said. "Wait a little while and the fruit will fall into your hand. You must be patient, Esperanza."
<atomic>She waited and lay silent, watching Papa's eyes. And then she felt it. Softly at first. A gentle thumping. Then stronger. A resounding thud, thud, thud against her body.</atomic>
She could hear it, too. The beat rushing in her ears. Shoomp, shoomp, shoomp.
<atomic>She stared at Papa, not wanting to say a word. Not wanting to lose the sound. Not wanting to forget the feel of the heart of the valley.</atomic>
<atomic>She pressed closer to the ground, until her body was breathing with the earth's. And with Papa's.</atomic>
<atomic><citation>From Pam Muñoz Ryan, Esperanza Rising. Copyright 2000 by Pam Muñoz Ryan</citation></atomic>

textContent.text: Esperanza's grandmother, whom everyone called Abuelita, lived with them and was a smaller, older, more wrinkled version of Mama. She looked very distinguished, wearing a respectable black dress, the same gold loops she wore in her ears every day, and her white hair pulled back into a bun at the nape of her neck. But Esperanza loved her more for her capricious ways than for her propriety. Abuelita might host a group of ladies for a formal tea in the afternoon, then after they had gone, be found wandering barefoot in the grapes, with a book in her hand, quoting poetry to the birds. Although some things were always the same with Abuelita—a lace-edged handkerchief peeking out from beneath the sleeve of her dress—others were surprising: a flower in her hair, a beautiful stone in her pocket, or a philosophical saying salted into her conversation. When Abuelita walked into a room, everyone scrambled to make her comfortable. Even Papa would give up his chair for her.
Esperanza complained, "Must we always crochet to take our minds off worry?" She sat next to her grandmother anyway, smelling her ever-present aroma of garlic, face powder, and peppermint.
"What happened to your finger?" asked Abuelita.
"A big thorn," said Esperanza.

pieces.text: Abuelita nodded and said thoughtfully, "
There is no rose without thorns."

textContent.text: Esperanza smiled, knowing that Abuelita wasn't talking about flowers at all but that there was no life without difficulties. She watched the silver crochet needle dance back and forth in her grandmother's hand. When a strand of hair fell into her lap, Abuelita picked it up and held it against the yarn and stitched it into the blanket.

"Esperanza, in this way my love and good wishes will be in the blanket forever. Now watch. Ten stitches up to the top of the mountain. Add one stitch. Nine stitches down to the bottom of the valley. Skip one."

Esperanza picked up her own crochet needle and copied Abuelita's movements and then looked at her own crocheting. The tops of her mountains were lopsided and the bottoms of her valleys were all bunched up. Abuelita smiled, reached over, and pulled the yarn, unraveling all of Esperanza's rows. "Do not be afraid to start over," she said.
Esperanza sighed and began again with ten stitches.

content.text: Reread the following passage from Esperanza Rising. In this excerpt, Esperanza and her father walk through the family vineyard near their home in Aguascalientes, Mexico.

textContent.text: "Our land is alive, Esperanza," said Papa, taking her small hand as they walked through the gentle slopes of the vineyard. Leafy green vines draped the arbors and the grapes were ready to drop. Esperanza was six years old and loved to walk with her papa through the winding rows, gazing up at him and watching his eyes dance with love for the land.

"This whole valley breathes and lives," he said, sweeping his arm toward the distant mountains that guarded them. "It gives us the grapes and then they welcome us." He gently touched a wild tendril that reached into the row, as if it had been waiting to shake his hand. He picked up a handful of earth and studied it. "Did you know that when you lie down on the land, you can feel it breathe? That you can feel its heart beating?"
"Papi, I want to feel it," she said.
"Come." They walked to the end of the row, where the incline of the land formed a grassy swell.
Papa lay down on his stomach and looked up at her, patting the ground next to him.

Esperanza smoothed her dress and knelt down. Then, like a caterpillar, she slowly inched flat next to him, their faces looking at each other. The warm sun pressed on one of Esperanza's cheeks and the warm earth on the other.
She giggled.
"Shhh," he said. "You can only feel the earth's heartbeat when you are still and quiet."
She swallowed her laughter and after a moment said, "I can't hear it, Papi."

content.text: In the novel, the characters of Abuelita and Esperanza possess traits similar to those of Muñoz Ryan's grandmother.

pieces.text: Some of the events are also drawn from real-life experiences Muñoz Ryan had with her grandmother.

content.text: For instance, Muñoz Ryan's grandmother taught her how to crochet using the same mountain and valley technique featured in the novel.

pieces.text: When Muñoz Ryan became an adult, she learned more about her grandmother's life. Muñoz Ryan recalls being surprised to know that her grandmother had been living like a princess in Mexico.

content.text: Her grandmother had been born into a wealthy family, but just like the fictional Esperanza, had to give it all up when she moved to work on the farm labor camps in California.

text.text: <atomic>Esperanza's grandmother, whom everyone called Abuelita, lived with them and was a smaller, older, more wrinkled version of Mama. She looked very distinguished, wearing a respectable black dress, the same gold loops she wore in her ears every day, and her white hair pulled back into a bun at the nape of her neck. But Esperanza loved her more for her capricious ways than for her propriety.</atomic>

<atomic>Abuelita might host a group of ladies for a formal tea in the afternoon, then after they had gone, be found wandering barefoot in the grapes, with a book in her hand, quoting poetry to the birds.</atomic>

<atomic>Although some things were always the same with Abuelita—a lace-edged handkerchief peeking out from beneath the sleeve of her dress—others were surprising: a flower in her hair, a beautiful stone in her pocket, or a philosophical saying salted into her conversation.</atomic>
<atomic>When Abuelita walked into a room, everyone scrambled to make her comfortable. Even Papa would give up his chair for her.</atomic>

<atomic>Esperanza complained, "Must we always crochet to take our minds off worry?" She sat next to her grandmother anyway, smelling her ever-present aroma of garlic, face powder, and peppermint.</atomic>
<atomic>"What happened to your finger?" asked Abuelita.</atomic>
<atomic>"A big thorn," said Esperanza.</atomic>
Abuelita nodded and said thoughtfully, "No hay rosa sin espinas. There is no rose without thorns."
<atomic>Esperanza smiled, knowing that Abuelita wasn't talking about flowers at all but that there was no life without difficulties.</atomic>

<atomic>She watched the silver crochet needle dance back and forth in her grandmother's hand. When a strand of hair fell into her lap, Abuelita picked it up and held it against the yarn and stitched it into the blanket.</atomic>

<atomic>"Esperanza, in this way my love and good wishes will be in the blanket forever. Now watch. Ten stitches up to the top of the mountain. Add one stitch. Nine stitches down to the bottom of the valley. Skip one."</atomic>

<atomic>Esperanza picked up her own crochet needle and copied Abuelita's movements and then looked at her own crocheting. The tops of her mountains were lopsided and the bottoms of her valleys were all bunched up.</atomic>
<atomic>Abuelita smiled, reached over, and pulled the yarn, unraveling all of Esperanza's rows. "Do not be afraid to start over," she said.</atomic>
<atomic>Esperanza sighed and began again with ten stitches.</atomic>
<atomic><citation>From Pam Muñoz Ryan, Esperanza Rising. Copyright 2000 by Pam Muñoz Ryan</citation></atomic>

content.text: Read the following passage from Esperanza Rising. In this excerpt, Esperanza and her father walk through the family vineyard near their home in Aguascalientes, Mexico.

textContent.text: "Our land is alive, Esperanza," said Papa, taking her small hand as they walked through the gentle slopes of the vineyard. Leafy green vines draped the arbors and the grapes were ready to drop. Esperanza was six years old and loved to walk with her papa through the winding rows, gazing up at him and watching his eyes dance with love for the land.

"This whole valley breathes and lives," he said, sweeping his arm toward the distant mountains that guarded them. "It gives us the grapes and then they welcome us." He gently touched a wild tendril that reached into the row, as if it had been waiting to shake his hand. He picked up a handful of earth and studied it. "Did you know that when you lie down on the land, you can feel it breathe? That you can feel its heart beating?"
"Papi, I want to feel it," she said.
"Come." They walked to the end of the row, where the incline of the land formed a grassy swell.
Papa lay down on his stomach and looked up at her, patting the ground next to him.

Esperanza smoothed her dress and knelt down. Then, like a caterpillar, she slowly inched flat next to him, their faces looking at each other. The warm sun pressed on one of Esperanza's cheeks and the warm earth on the other.
She giggled.
"Shhh," he said. "You can only feel the earth's heartbeat when you are still and quiet."
She swallowed her laughter and after a moment said, "I can't hear it, Papi."

content.text: "Aguantate tantito y la fruta caerá en tu mano,"

pieces.text: he said. "Wait a little while and the fruit will fall into your hand. You must be patient, Esperanza."

textContent.text: She waited and lay silent, watching Papa's eyes. And then she felt it. Softly at first. A gentle thumping. Then stronger. A resounding thud, thud, thud against her body.

pieces.text: She could hear it, too. The beat rushing in her ears.

textContent.text: She stared at Papa, not wanting to say a word. Not wanting to lose the sound. Not wanting to forget the feel of the heart of the valley.
She pressed closer to the ground, until her body was breathing with the earth's. And with Papa's.
<citation>From Pam Muñoz Ryan, Esperanza Rising. Copyright 2000 by Pam Muñoz Ryan</citation>

She looked very distinguished, wearing a respectable black dress, the same gold loops she wore in her ears every day, and her white hair pulled back into a bun at the nape of her neck. But Esperanza loved her more for her capricious ways than for her propriety. Abuelita might host a group of ladies for a formal tea in the afternoon, then after they had gone, be found wandering barefoot in the grapes, with a book in her hand, quoting poetry to the birds. Although some things were always the same with Abuelita—a lace-edged handkerchief peeking out from beneath the sleeve of her dress—others were surprising: a flower in her hair, a beautiful stone in her pocket, or a philosophical saying salted into her conversation. When Abuelita walked into a room, everyone scrambled to make her comfortable. Even Papa would give up his chair for her.
Esperanza complained, "Must we always crochet to take our minds off worry?" She sat next to her grandmother anyway, smelling her ever-present aroma of garlic, face powder, and peppermint.
"What happened to your finger?" asked Abuelita.
"A big thorn," said Esperanza.

pieces.text: Abuelita nodded and said thoughtfully, "
There is no rose without thorns."

textContent.text: Esperanza smiled, knowing that Abuelita wasn't talking about flowers at all but that there was no life without difficulties. She watched the silver crochet needle dance back and forth in her grandmother's hand. When a strand of hair fell into her lap, Abuelita picked it up and held it against the yarn and stitched it into the blanket.

"Esperanza, in this way my love and good wishes will be in the blanket forever. Now watch. Ten stitches up to the top of the mountain. Add one stitch. Nine stitches down to the bottom of the valley. Skip one."

Esperanza picked up her own crochet needle and copied Abuelita's movements and then looked at her own crocheting. The tops of her mountains were lopsided and the bottoms of her valleys were all bunched up. Abuelita smiled, reached over, and pulled the yarn, unraveling all of Esperanza's rows. "Do not be afraid to start over," she said.
Esperanza sighed and began again with ten stitches.

pieces.text: Author Pam Muñoz Ryan had a grandmother who lived in Aguascalientes, Mexico and was named Esperanza Ortega.

content.text: In the novel, the characters of Abuelita and Esperanza possess traits similar to those of Muñoz Ryan's grandmother.

pieces.text: Some of the events are also drawn from real-life experiences Muñoz Ryan had with her grandmother.

content.text: For instance, Muñoz Ryan's grandmother taught her how to crochet using the same mountain and valley technique featured in the novel.

pieces.text: When Muñoz Ryan became an adult, she learned more about her grandmother's life. Muñoz Ryan recalls being surprised to know that her grandmother had been living like a princess in Mexico.

content.text: Her grandmother had been born into a wealthy family, but just like the fictional Esperanza, had to give it all up when she moved to work on the farm labor camps in California.
